references.text: David's psalm about the suffering one who is mocked by the people: "All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me, they shake their heads: 'He has committed himself to the Lord; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!'" ([ref:Sal 22:7-8|Psalms 22:7-8]). This is a prophetic text about the Messiah being mocked, which was directly fulfilled at the crucifixion.
In [ref:Sal 22:17-18|Psalms 22:17-18], the suffering one is described as surrounded by enemies who stare and look at him, paralleling how the people stood and watched Jesus on the cross.

Matthew's parallel account of the mockery at the cross: "Those who passed by reviled him... 'He trusts in God; let God deliver him now'" ([ref:Matt 27:39-43|Matthew 27:39-43]). It contains the same motif of mockery from the people and leaders.
Mark's parallel account of the mockery at the cross ([ref:Mark 15:29-32|Mark 15:29-32]), where also the chief priests and scribes mock Jesus, saying that he saved others but cannot save himself.

God's chosen servant is mentioned in [ref:Jes 42:1|Isaiah 42:1]: "Behold my servant... my chosen." Luke uses the expression "the Chosen One" (ὁ ἐκλεκτός) about Jesus, connecting to Isaiah's prophecy concerning the Lord's servant.

At the transfiguration on the mountain, a voice from the cloud says: "This is my Son, the Chosen One" ([ref:Luk 9:35|Luke 9:35]). The same designation "the Chosen One" is used here as in the mockery at the cross, an ironic contrast.
In [ref:Luk 4:23|Luke 4:23], Jesus says that people will say to him: "Doctor, heal yourself!" This has a thematic parallel to the mockery "he saved others; let him save himself."
The Lord's suffering servant is "despised and rejected by men" ([ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]). The mockery from the people and leaders at the cross fulfills this prophecy.
In [ref:Sal 69:21|Psalms 69:21], the suffering one is described as waiting for compassion but finding none – a parallel to how the people only stood and watched while the leaders mocked Jesus.

The mockery from the leaders continues with the soldiers in [ref:Luk 23:36-37|Luke 23:36-37], who also mock him, saying: "If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!" – the same pattern of mockery linked to salvation.

In [ref:Matt 1:21|Matthew 1:21], Jesus receives his name because "he will save his people from their sins." The mockery "he saved others" ironically confirms Jesus' identity as Savior, even though the mockers intended it as an insult.
In [ref:1 Pet 2:4|1 Peter 2:4], Jesus is described as "the living stone... chosen and precious to God," connecting to the designation "God's Chosen One" in Luke 23:35.
